opus-5.5.text:
I think both have essential roles, and the mistake would be to think that one makes the other obsolete.

Big science, in the sense of large teams, large compute, and large datasets, has clearly shown its power over the last decade. When you scale up models like large language models or big vision systems, you get capabilities that you simply could not have predicted from small experiments. That kind of work needs industrial resources, and companies like Google, Meta, and OpenAI are well positioned to do it. Physics went through a similar transition. You can't build the Large Hadron Collider in a university basement.

But I'd caution against concluding that all progress will come from scale. Many of the core ideas we rely on today came from small groups, often a professor and a few graduate students, trying something unconventional. Convolutional networks, backpropagation, much of reinforcement learning, many of the ideas in self-supervised learning: these started as small science. Academia's comparative advantage is the freedom to work on problems that aren't fashionable and to take intellectual risks that wouldn't make sense for a product roadmap.

There's also a role for small science in understanding. Big systems work, but we often don't know why, or where they'll fail. Careful, controlled experiments, sometimes inspired by cognitive science or child development, can tell us a lot. I've long felt we should look at how children learn: through embodied interaction, multimodal experience, and play, rather than passively absorbing enormous text corpora. Exploring those ideas doesn't necessarily need ten thousand GPUs at first.

So the healthy ecosystem is one where small groups generate and test ideas cheaply, and the promising ones get scaled up by groups with more resources. Then scaling reveals new phenomena and limitations, which feed back into new questions for the small groups. What worries me is if academic researchers feel they can't contribute unless they match industrial compute, and abandon the questions they're best suited to ask. That would be a loss for the whole field.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think both have a role, and I'd resist the framing that one has made the other obsolete. Big science in AI today looks like training enormous models on enormous amounts of data with enormous amounts of compute, and that's produced genuinely remarkable results. I'm not going to pretend otherwise. But big science is fundamentally about scaling up ideas that already exist. It's engineering of a very high order, and it requires the kind of resources that only a handful of industrial labs have.

Small science is where the ideas come from in the first place. If you look at the history of the field, the key conceptual advances, convolutional networks, backpropagation, the basic architecture of attention, these came out of small groups, often in universities, often working on what at the time looked like toy problems. Nobody needed ten thousand GPUs to have those ideas. And I'd argue that the questions that matter most right now, how do we learn from very little data the way a child does, how do we get common sense, how do we connect perception to action in the physical world, those are not going to be solved simply by scaling. They need new ideas, and new ideas come from people who have the freedom to be wrong for a few years.

So my view is that universities should not try to compete with industry at big science. We'll lose, and we should be honest about that. What we should do is the thing industry is structurally bad at, which is taking intellectual risks that don't have a product attached, training the next generation of researchers, and asking the uncomfortable questions about whether the current paradigm actually works. There's a healthy division of labor there if we're willing to accept it. The danger is that students and young faculty get the impression that the only respectable work is work at scale, and then the pipeline of new ideas dries up. That would be bad for everybody, including the big labs.

r003.rationale: It presents small science as the source of new ideas and says researchers need freedom to take intellectual risks, supporting exploration.

r004.rationale: It explicitly describes big science as scaling up ideas that already exist.

r005.rationale: It distinguishes universities from industry labs, but says universities should not try to compete in big science rather than identifying academic research as capable of operating at that scale.

astra-6.text:
I think we need both. Small science is where an individual or a small group can pursue an idea that is quite different from what everybody else is doing. You can question the formulation of a problem, try a new approach, and do an experiment that tells you whether the idea makes sense. That freedom is very important.

Big science lets you explore questions that require substantial resources—large datasets, large amounts of computation, and teams with different kinds of expertise. There are things you simply cannot learn by working at a small scale.

The danger is to equate the amount of resources used with the quality of the science. A large experiment is not automatically a good experiment. You still need to ask: What did we learn? Which hypothesis did we test? And a clever idea demonstrated on a small problem still needs to confront the complexity of the real world.

So I see them as complementary. We need the capacity to build and test at scale, but we also need room for people with modest resources to challenge the assumptions behind what we are building.

sol-6.1.text:
I think there is a role for both. Small science is where an individual or a small group can explore an idea, question an assumption, and try something that may be quite different from what everybody else is doing. You want to preserve that freedom, particularly in universities.

Big science becomes valuable when the question requires resources that a small group cannot assemble—large amounts of computation, data, or a substantial engineering effort. It lets you investigate things at a scale that would otherwise be impossible.

The mistake would be to assume that scale is the only source of progress. A large experiment can be very useful, but so can a small experiment that reveals that we have been asking the wrong question. So I would want an ecosystem that supports both, with ideas moving between them.
